svg.title: How observed dependencies become move groups, and move groups become waves
svg.desc: Discovery collects observed connections. Shared services such as Active Directory, DNS, monitoring and backup are built in the target first and excluded from grouping, because a dependency common to every application would group the entire estate into one unit. Genuine couplings such as a shared database, an ETL job, a common owner or a shared patch window bind servers into a move group, which is never split. Move groups are packed into waves capped at fifty servers, with the first waves under ten, sized against a four-architect team migrating up to fifty servers a week.
svg.text: LAYER 1 — WHAT COMMUNICATES (COLLECTED, NOT DECIDED)
Observed inbound and outbound connections per server, over long enough to catch the monthly jobs
The CMDB records what was built and who owned it. Traffic records what is actually running. Neither is sufficient alone.
LAYER 2 — WHAT MUST NOT BE SEPARATED (THE JUDGEMENT)
Shared services — build first, then ignore
Active Directory · DNS · NTP · monitoring
backup · certificate authority · patching
AWS: a dependency on Active Directory
“should not be considered when defining
move groups” — it is common to all
Built in the target before wave 1, so it binds nothing.
Couplings — these bind a move group
shared database · ETL job · shared file store
same application owner · same patch window
the last two are not technical at all,
and are what reschedules a wave
A move group is never split. Ever.
LAYER 3 — PACKING MOVE GROUPS INTO WAVES
Waves 1–5
Under 10 servers. Dev and test.
Low complexity. Deliberately dull.
the first cutover teaches an
expensive lesson either way
Steady state
Cap 50 servers per wave, sized to
what the team can actually absorb.
AWS measure: 4 architects,
up to 50 servers a week, rehost
Horizon
Plan 4 to 5 waves ahead, not thirty.
Wave planning is continuous.
early waves change later ones;
a full plan turns that into slippage
THE FAILURE THIS PREVENTS
A move group split across two waves is a Saturday morning rollback
The application comes up in the target and cannot reach a database still on-premises, owned by another team, scheduled for wave 9.
If one move group exceeds the 50-server cap on its own, that is a finding about the architecture, not a packing problem — escalate it
rather than splitting the group.
